name: Prompt & Tool Controls
question: Is the agent using more tokens and calls than it needs?
summary: Put limits and lean defaults on what each request can consume: concise system prompts, capped output length, fewer and tighter tool definitions, compact tool results, and a cap on how many steps an agent loop can take. Agents are expensive mostly because they loop and carry bulky tool output from step to step.
useCases: Agent loops with many tool calls per task
Tools that return large payloads: search results, logs, full records
Prompts that grew over time with duplicated instructions

items.detail: maximum iterations or tool calls per task
expose only the tools relevant to this task
return IDs and summaries, not full payloads
remove duplicated rules and unused examples
a JSON schema instead of verbose prose

steps: Measure tokens per step and find the biggest contributors
Set max_tokens and a step budget per task type, with a graceful stop
Load tool definitions dynamically so each call carries only what it needs
Trim tool responses at the source: paginate, filter fields, summarize
pitfalls: Caps set too low truncate answers or stop tasks halfway
Cutting examples can quietly lower quality, so re-run your evals
Dynamic tool loading adds a selection step that can choose wrong
remember: Budget every loop. Trim every payload.
caption: Each block is one step, sized by its tokens. Controls cut both the number of steps and their size.

code.text: keep = {k: result[k] for k in ("pan", "name", "dob", "page") if k in result}
return json.dumps(keep)                  # fields, not the raw OCR text
system=SYSTEM + " Reply with the JSON fields only.",
log_usage(task_type, step, resp.usage)   # tokens per step
# Nightly: rerun the KYC eval set, compare tokens per task and pass rate

steps.title: Measure tokens per step
steps.text: Log usage on every step. This KYC task takes 8 steps and 52k tokens, and each step is bigger than the last because context accumulates.

steps.title: Load only the tools the task needs
steps.text: All 14 tool definitions ride along on every call. KYC needs 3, so load those and drop the rest.

steps.title: Cap and shape the output
steps.text: Set max_tokens per task type and ask for JSON fields instead of prose. Replies fall from about 900 tokens to 250.

steps.title: Trim tool results at the source
steps.text: The page reader returned 3,000 tokens of raw OCR text. Return only the fields the next step needs: about 600 tokens.

steps.title: Set a step budget with a graceful stop
steps.text: Cap the loop at 6 steps. If the budget runs out, return a partial result for review instead of looping on.

steps.title: Re-run the evals
steps.text: Tokens per task fall from 52k to 11k. The KYC eval pass rate holds at 94%, so the controls cost no quality.

pros: Caps the worst case: runaway loops can no longer run up the bill
Fewer tokens per step also means faster steps
Mostly code in your own agent loop, no new vendor
Makes cost per task predictable enough to budget
cons: Caps set too low stop tasks halfway
Trimming can remove information a later step needed
Dynamic tool loading adds a selection step that can pick wrong
Every change needs an eval re-run to confirm quality
avoidWhen: Single-call features with short prompts (little to control)
You can’t yet measure tokens per step (instrument first)

playgroundGuide.scenario: A KYC document agent checks identity documents. A clean run needs 5 steps, but some runs get stuck re-reading pages and loop until something stops them. You decide the step budget and which controls are on: loading only the tools the task needs, trimming tool results, and capping output.
controls: Drag the slider to set the step budget (15 means no budget: the platform stops runs at 15).
Tick the controls to switch on tool pruning, trimmed tool results and concise output.
Or load a scenario to compare common setups.

outputs.meaning: Share of runs that finish the 5 steps the task needs.

outputs.meaning: Each chip is one step, sized in tokens. Red chips are wasted or unfinished steps.

outputs.meaning: All input and output tokens for a normal 5-step run.

presets.expect: 30% of runs loop to 15 steps. Average cost $0.729 per task, 70% of tasks completed.

presets.name: Budget of 10 only
presets.expect: Loops stop at 10 steps: cost falls 36% to $0.466, completion stays at 70%.

presets.name: All controls, budget 6
presets.expect: Loops drop to 5% of runs and every step is smaller: $0.086 per task, 88% cheaper, 95% completed.

presets.name: Budget too tight

missions.text: Using only the step budget, cut cost by at least 40% without losing completed tasks.
missions.hint: Turn off the other controls and lower the budget to 8 or below, but not under 5.

missions.text: Find the tightest step budget that still completes at least 90% of tasks.
missions.hint: The task needs 5 steps, and trimmed tool results cut loops to 5% of runs.

missions.text: With no budget, show that loading 3 tools instead of 14 saves more than 10% on its own.
missions.hint: Set the budget to 15, turn on only the tool control.

cons: A spend cap stops work abruptly; it is not a step budget

tools.ex: Measure that a raw OCR page is 3,000 tokens and the extracted fields are 150, before changing the tool.
pros: Fast and exact for OpenAI tokenizers
cons: Counts tokens, does not enforce anything

practice.scenario: A KYC document agent sometimes looped 15 times, re-reading the same PDF pages with all 14 tools loaded. The fix: cap it at 6 steps, load only the 3 tools KYC needs, trim each tool result to a short summary, and set max_tokens per step. The team then re-runs the KYC eval set to confirm the pass rate holds.

industries.use: Bound document-review loops and trim OCR payloads
Cap reply length per channel, such as SMS versus email
Return only failing test lines instead of full logs

numericDrill.question: Steps use 4k, 5k, 6k, 7k, 8k, 9k, 10k and 11k tokens. You set a step budget of 5 and trim tool output so each step is 30% smaller. Total tokens after, in thousands?
numericDrill.answer: Before: 60k. After: the first five steps (4+5+6+7+8 = 30k) × 0.7 = 21k, about a third of the original.

interview.question: Why are agents so much more expensive than single LLM calls?
interview.answer: Each step resends the growing context, tool definitions and earlier tool outputs, so tokens compound across steps, and loops can run long. Step budgets, trimmed tool output and fewer loaded tools attack the compounding.

interview.question: How do you choose max_tokens?
interview.answer: Measure the output-length distribution per task type on real traffic, set the cap a little above the 95th–99th percentile, and handle truncation gracefully.

mistakes.mistake: One global max_tokens for every task
mistakes.fix: Set caps per task type from measured lengths

mistakes.mistake: Returning raw API payloads to the model
mistakes.fix: Return only the fields the next step needs

quiz.question: A KYC agent sometimes loops 15 times re-reading the same PDF pages. What is the most direct control?
options: A step budget with a graceful stop
quiz.explanation: A step budget caps the loop, and a graceful stop returns a useful partial result instead of failing.

quiz.question: A coding agent’s 8 steps use 2k, 4k, 6k … 16k tokens. You set a budget of 5 steps and trim tool output so each step is 40% smaller. Total tokens now?
quiz.explanation: The first five steps are 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 30k; 40% smaller gives 30k × 0.6 = 18k, down from 72k.

quiz.question: Which changes reduce the tokens carried by each step of an agent? Select all that apply.
options: Returning only the needed fields from tools
quiz.explanation: Fewer tool definitions, compact results and short outputs all shrink a step. The budget limits the number of steps, not their size.

quiz.question: Measured replies for order-status questions have a 99th-percentile length of 320 tokens. How should you set max_tokens?
options: A little above 320, and handle truncated replies gracefully
quiz.explanation: Set the cap from measured lengths with a small margin, and handle the rare truncation.

quiz.question: Twenty tool definitions of 450 tokens each ride along on each of 12 calls in a task. Loading only 4 tools saves how many input tokens per task?
quiz.explanation: 16 unneeded tools × 450 tokens × 12 calls = 86,400 tokens per task.

quiz.question: Removing examples from a clause-extraction prompt cut cost 20%, but accuracy fell from 95% to 88%. What is the lesson?
options: Re-run evals after trimming, and restore the examples that mattered
quiz.explanation: Prompt cuts can quietly lower quality. Evals show which cuts were free and which were not.

quiz.question: A triage agent loads tools dynamically, and 3% of requests get billing tools instead of scheduling tools. What should you add?
options: Load all 40 tools on every call
Remove tool descriptions to save tokens
Evals for the tool-selection step and a way to request more tools
quiz.explanation: Dynamic loading adds a selection step that can be wrong. Test it and give the agent a fallback.

quiz.question: Which are real cost drivers in agent loops? Select all that apply.
options: Tool outputs accumulate in the context
Tool definitions are resent on every step
Each extra step resends the whole history
quiz.explanation: Agents compound cost because every step resends a growing context. Output tokens are usually the most expensive kind.

quiz.question: Output costs $15 per million tokens. Replies shrink from 900 to 250 tokens on 10,000 replies a day. What is the daily saving?
quiz.explanation: 650 fewer tokens × 10,000 = 6.5M tokens × $15/M = $97.50 a day.

quiz.question: A market-data tool returns 500 rows of ticks, but the agent only needs the latest price. What should the tool return?
options: A summary of the ticks from another LLM call every time
The latest price and timestamp, with a way to fetch more
quiz.explanation: Compact tool results keep every later step small; an option to fetch more covers rare needs.

quiz.question: You need a per-step breakdown of tokens and cost for every agent trace, self-hosted for data residency. Which tool fits?
quiz.explanation: Langfuse traces each step with token counts and cost and can be self-hosted.

quiz.question: You want to count tokens locally for OpenAI models before sending a prompt. What do you use?
quiz.explanation: tiktoken is OpenAI’s tokenizer library and counts tokens without a network call.

quiz.question: What should happen when an agent reaches its step budget? Select all that apply.
options: Return a partial result with what was done
Log the reason for later review
Flag the task for a person or a retry
quiz.explanation: A graceful stop keeps the work useful and visible. Ignoring the budget defeats it.

quiz.question: Normal runs take 5 steps; 20% of runs loop to 20 steps. Each step costs $0.02. What is the average cost per run with a budget of 8 steps?
quiz.explanation: Normal: 0.8 × 5 × $0.02 = $0.08. Looping, capped at 8: 0.2 × 8 × $0.02 = $0.032. Total $0.112, against $0.16 with no budget.

quiz.question: A tutor bot has max_tokens 150, and some answers stop mid-sentence. What is the fix?
options: Set the cap a little above the measured length of complete answers and handle max_tokens stops
quiz.explanation: Caps set below real answer lengths truncate work. Measure, add a margin and handle the stop reason.

quiz.question: A rebooking agent writes 400-token prose confirmations that a program then parses. What is the lean fix?
options: Ask for JSON with only the needed fields
Use a larger model for better prose
quiz.explanation: Structured output removes verbose prose and makes parsing reliable.

quiz.question: Which are signs that an agent is missing prompt and tool controls? Select all that apply.
options: The 99th-percentile steps per task are six times the median
Tool results over 5,000 tokens that are used once
Each task loads 30 tool definitions but uses 2
quiz.explanation: Long-tail loops, bulky one-use tool output and unused tool definitions are the classic waste. A high hit rate is good news.

quiz.question: A tenant’s key has a monthly spend limit of $500 and has spent $480. A runaway agent would spend $60 more. With a hard limit, how much more can it spend?
quiz.explanation: The limit stops spend at $500, so at most $20 more. It is a safety net under your own step budgets.

quiz.question: Which limits bound the cost of a single agent task? Select all that apply.
options: A per-key spend limit as a safety net
quiz.explanation: Steps, output per step and a spend ceiling each cap part of the cost. Temperature does not.

quiz.question: A claims task needs 5 steps, but the step budget is 3, and no task completes. What is wrong?
options: The budget is below what the task needs; set it from the steps successful runs take
quiz.explanation: Caps set too low stop tasks halfway. Base the budget on measured successful runs, with a margin.
